title: Axia: an open-source web interface and REST API for Active Directory and OpenLDAP
summary:
Every company with a directory has the same routine: create an account, reset a password, add someone to a group, disable a leaver. That work belongs with helpdesk or HR. But the usual ways of handing it over are RSAT on a domain-joined machine, an LDAP client, or a PowerShell script that someone has to maintain. And in all of them, the hard part is making sure helpdesk can't quietly promote itself.
We built Nelsar.Axia for that: a self-hosted web interface and REST API for Active Directory, Samba AD, OpenLDAP and eDirectory. It's open source under Apache 2.0.
What it does
• Users, groups, OUs and computer accounts. Search, create, edit and delete them from the browser, and read raw attributes when you need them.
• Several directories at once. One instance can serve AD and OpenLDAP side by side, and each session stays bound to the directory it signed in to.
• Roles from directory groups. You map a group like cn=helpdesk,ou=groups,... to a role, and the role to a set of 17 permissions. Take someone out of the group, and half a minute later the rights are gone.
• Bulk provisioning. Create accounts in batches, with a login generator that transliterates names (Cyrillic to Latin, for example) and checks every login against the directory before anything is written.
• An audit log. It records every sign-in and every change, including refused attempts, with who made them.
• A REST API with OpenAPI. Onboarding and offboarding scripts can call it instead of speaking LDAP.
• Nine interface languages, including Arabic and Hebrew with a mirrored layout.
The part we spent the most time on
Axia talks to the directory through one service account with broad rights and decides on its own who may do what. That's how most delegation tools work, and it has a price. The directory no longer protects your admins, because all it ever sees is the service account. AdminSDHolder, OU delegation and olcAccess all stop helping.
So the protection has to live in the application:
• Nobody can act on anyone who holds more rights than they do. "More" is measured in Axia's roles and in the directory itself: members of protected groups, found by SID and resolved through nesting and primary groups. A helpdesk role that can reset passwords can't reset a Domain Admin's.
• Moving or renaming an OU counts as a permission change. If the OU holds a group that grants a role, only someone who already holds that role's rights can move it.
• Repointing a directory connection requires the bind password again. Without this rule, anyone who could edit a connection could send the stored service account password to a host of their choosing (LDAP pass-back).
• Brute force through the console can't lock accounts in AD. A lockout in the directory blocks new sign-ins but doesn't end live sessions, so nobody can kick an admin out by typing wrong passwords. Failed sign-ins are capped per account below the directory's own threshold.
• Passwords are written the way the directory expects: unicodePwd over an encrypted connection for AD, and the Password Modify extended operation for OpenLDAP. Never as a plain userPassword attribute.
We wrote up how each of these was found, along with the code, in a longer article: How a helpdesk role could take over the admin: five traps in a web console for Active Directory and OpenLDAP.
Try it in a few minutes
All you need is Docker with Compose v2:
git clone https://github.com/Nelsar/Axia.git
cd Axia
docker compose up
Open http://localhost:8080. The demo comes with an OpenLDAP that has an account for every role, and every password is Axia-Demo-1. The most telling test: sign in as editor.demo and try to reset admin.demo's password.
For real deployments, there are images on ghcr.io and Docker Hub (nelsar/axia-api, nelsar/axia-console) for amd64 and arm64. There's also a Windows installer that runs Axia as a service with nothing else to install. It stores its data in PostgreSQL or SQLite.
What it doesn't do yet
Axia is an MVP at version 0.3, and we'd rather you hear the gaps from us:
• No sign-out or token revocation. A session token lives 60 minutes. Disabling the account in the directory ends the session within 30 seconds.
• No two-factor authentication or OpenID Connect sign-in yet. Both are next on the roadmap: TOTP required by role, and sign-in through Entra ID, AD FS or Keycloak.
• No revocation checks (CRL, OCSP) for directory certificates.
• One instance only. Bulk jobs and sign-in counters live in memory.
The Windows installer isn't code-signed yet. Each release carries a build provenance attestation instead, which gh attestation verify checks.
Links
• Source: github.com/Nelsar/Axia
• Documentation: nelsar.github.io/Axia
If you run OpenLDAP or Samba in production, we'd especially like to hear what breaks. Issues are open on GitHub. And if you hand directory work to helpdesk today, how do you do it: delegation, a commercial tool, or scripts?

title: Choosing an Overseas VPS: Nodes and Network First, Specs Second
summary:
Once you start running overseas accounts or tools seriously, one question comes up fast: where do the tools live? A local machine goes to sleep, a phone is unstable, and a shared machine cross-contaminates environments. A VPS solves the uptime problem. It does not solve the account problem, and confusing the two is where most people waste money.

What the server is actually for

Think of it as a three-piece stack. The account is the identity. The IP is the address the account shows to the platform. The server is where the tools run. A clean IP fixes attribution. A stable server fixes uptime. You need both, and they need to agree: the server node, the account region, and the IP country should line up. A US account logging in from a Tokyo node through a mismatched IP looks inconsistent no matter how clean each piece is on its own.

Nodes first, specs second

Most buyers start with CPU and RAM. Start with location instead.

Pick a node in the same country as the accounts you run. US accounts go on a Los Angeles node, Japan-related work on Tokyo, and Hong Kong fits when you need low latency to mainland China. The provider I use, 8E Cloud, offers exactly those three nodes: Los Angeles, Hong Kong, and Tokyo. Buy the wrong region because it was cheaper, and your login geography jumps around, which is visible to every platform you touch.

The line matters more than the spec

How you connect to the server matters more than how fast the server is. A cheap VPS on congested transit feels fine at noon and falls apart at peak hours, with latency spikes and packet loss right when you need remote desktop or file transfers to work.

This is why carriers matter. China Telecom's CN2 GIA is a premium backbone built for low latency and low loss, and on 8E it is the Premium network profile. Match the line to the workload: remote desktop, media uploads, and real-time tooling need a good line; a light cron job does not. Paying for premium transit on a box that only runs scheduled scripts is wasted money, and running interactive work over budget transit is false economy.

One practical tip: test the route at peak hours, not just once at noon. A single good ping tells you nothing about the evening.

Form factor: start small

Cloud instances, dedicated cloud, and physical machines are different products. A cloud instance spins up fast and is the right place to start. Dedicated cloud and physical machines give you exclusive resources, with physical machines offering uplinks up to 10Gbps, and they make sense once volume grows and environments need to stay separated. Start with a cloud instance, prove the setup works, then scale up. Buying the heaviest machine on day one just burns money while it idles.

Deployment speed and protection

Two things to confirm before you pay. First, deployment time: 8E deploys in minutes, so you can validate an environment the same day instead of waiting on manual provisioning. Second, DDoS protection. A server that stays online is a target, so protection should be standard, not an add-on. Confirm it covers the node and plan you actually pick, rather than assuming every tier includes it.

Buying smart

Validate small. One instance, one tool, one node, one week. Only expand after that works.

One more honesty note: 8E does not list prices on its homepage, so I will not quote any here. Confirm the total on the checkout page before you commit, since price varies by node and form factor. Full disclosure: if you try it, my invite code LH7777 at checkout takes 20% off the total order.

Pitfalls that keep showing up

  • One environment, too many accounts. A stable server does not protect you from correlated bans when dozens of accounts share one environment.
  • Using the server IP as the account IP. A datacenter IP and a residential IP are different things in a platform's eyes. The server runs tools; the account's traffic should go through a static residential IP.
  • Oversizing on day one. Servers bill by time, and an idle big machine is still a bill.
  • Expecting a server to fix behavior problems. Content violations, aggressive automation, and jumping IPs will still get accounts banned. A server fixes uptime and environment, nothing else.

Bottom line

Node first, line matched to workload, smallest form factor that works, protection confirmed, validated small before scaling. Get those five right and the server stops being the reason your setup breaks.

title: One instance per user, not per machine: a lock file that survives RDP reconnects
summary:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a Windows PC: you speak on the phone, and the text appears at the PC cursor over local Wi-Fi. The PC side is a small Node.js helper that sits in the tray, listens for the phone, and types.

It runs on an ordinary desktop, but also on a Windows Server that several people use through Remote Desktop at the same time. That second setup broke the single-instance guard twice, in two different ways. This is the guard as it stands now (src/singleInstance.js, 77 lines) and the two mistakes it fixes.

Why a second copy hurts

Two helpers in the same login don't just waste memory. They fight over the UDP port used for LAN discovery, both watch the clipboard, and each one doubles every child process. The phone can end up connected to whichever copy answered first. The symptom report is "it works sometimes".

Mistake 1: one instance per machine

The obvious guard is a machine-wide lock: a named mutex or a lock file in a shared folder. On a multi-user server that is wrong. Each person who logs in needs their own helper, typing into their own session. A machine-wide lock would let the first user's helper run and make everyone else's exit.

So the lock has to be per session. A lock file is enough here, and it is easy to reason about:

const fd = fs.openSync(lockPath, 'wx'); // exclusive create: fails if the file exists
fs.writeSync(fd, String(process.pid));
fs.closeSync(fd);

'wx' is the whole trick: creating the file is atomic, so two copies starting at the same moment cannot both succeed.

Mistake 2: keying the lock on SESSIONNAME

The first per-session version put %SESSIONNAME% into the lock file name. That looks right: on a Remote Desktop login it's something like RDP-Tcp#0.

It isn't stable. SESSIONNAME changes when the user disconnects and reconnects (RDP-Tcp#0 becomes RDP-Tcp#4), while the session itself, and the helper running in it, carries on. A relaunch after a reconnect looked for a lock under the new name, found none, and started a second helper beside the first. We saw exactly that on the server: one user, two helper PIDs, listening on two adjacent ports.

The fix was to key on the user instead:

const sessionKey = (process.env.USERNAME || os.userInfo().username || 'user')
  .replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/g, '_');
const lockPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `bolo-server-${sessionKey}.lock`);

On this server each user has one Windows session, so per-user is per-session. Two details make it robust:

  • os.tmpdir() is already per user, and on a Remote Desktop host it can even resolve to a per-session subfolder. The user name in the file name is belt and braces.
  • Sanitise the name. User names can contain characters you don't want in a file name. Replace them rather than trust them.

If your machines allow one user to have several simultaneous sessions, this key is too coarse; you would want the session id from the OS instead. Pick the key that matches how your machines are actually used, and write that assumption into the code comment, as this file does.

Stale locks: the PID check

A lock file outlives a crash. If the helper died without cleaning up, the next start finds the file and must decide whether its owner is still alive. The file holds the owner's PID, so:

function pidAlive(pid) {
  if (!pid || Number.isNaN(pid)) return false;
  try { process.kill(pid, 0); return true; }   // signal 0: existence check, kills nothing
  catch (e) { return e.code === 'EPERM'; }     // exists, but not ours to signal
}

process.kill(pid, 0) sends no signal; it only checks that the process exists. Note the EPERM branch: a process that exists but belongs to someone else throws EPERM, and that still means "alive". Treating every error as "dead" would let you steal a live lock.

If the holder is alive, the new copy logs one line naming the PID and exits. If not, it deletes the stale file and tries the exclusive create once more. Only once: if a third copy won the race in between, 'wx' fails again and the loop ends without spinning.

Never block startup on the guard itself

Two choices here are about failing open:

  • If creating the lock fails with anything other than EEXIST (a permissions problem, a missing temp folder), the helper logs a warning and starts anyway. A guard that stops the app from running at all is worse than an occasional duplicate.
  • On platforms where this guard isn't needed, it returns true immediately.

And cleanup is tied to the process: the lock is removed on exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM. A hard kill skips those, which is exactly what the PID check is for.

What carries over

  • Decide what "single" means (machine, user, or session) before choosing the lock.
  • Don't key a lock on a value that changes while the thing it protects keeps running. SESSIONNAME is one.
  • Use an atomic exclusive create ('wx') and store the PID inside.
  • process.kill(pid, 0) checks liveness; EPERM means alive.
  • Reclaim stale locks with one retry, not a loop.
  • When the guard itself fails, let the app start.

Bolo is on Google Play (search "Bolo AI"), and the Windows companion is on GitHub releases. The phone and PC talk over your local Wi-Fi.

title: The Risks of Leaving Environment Differences Implicit
summary:
The Risks of Leaving Environment Differences Implicit

An integration works in development. The API responds correctly, the application behaves as expected, and the developer is ready to deploy.

Then production behaves differently.

The cause might be different credentials, missing environment variables, different permissions, or configuration that was present during development but never reproduced in production.

These differences are not unusual. Development, testing, and production environments often serve different purposes.

The risk arises when developers do not understand which differences matter and what they must configure before moving between environments.

An integration that works in one environment does not automatically work in another.

How Environment Assumptions Develop

Consider a developer integrating a payment API.

During development, the application uses test credentials and successfully processes test transactions. The developer completes the main functionality and prepares for deployment.

However, production requires live credentials and the appropriate production configuration.

If the developer assumes that the existing setup carries over unchanged, the application may fail to perform live transactions until the missing configuration is corrected.

Stripe's documentation explicitly distinguishes test and live API keys and explains their different uses. The developer must use the appropriate credentials for the intended environment.

This is a documented product requirement, not evidence that Stripe customers generally misunderstand it.

The broader lesson applies to any product where environments differ in credentials, resources, permissions, endpoints, or configuration.

Why These Differences Can Be Overlooked

Developers often focus on getting the integration working before considering every deployment requirement.

A successful development environment can create confidence that the implementation is nearly complete.

But some requirements only become relevant when the application moves to another environment.

For example:

  • Development credentials may not be valid for production.
  • Environment variables may be missing from the deployment configuration.
  • Production permissions may differ from development permissions.
  • Resources created during testing may need to be created or configured separately.
  • Different endpoints or service settings may be required.

The problem is not that environments differ. It is that the implementation process may not make those differences sufficiently visible.

What Product Teams Should Examine

Product teams should investigate how developers move between environments and what they need to understand at each stage.

Useful questions include:

  1. Which settings and resources differ between environments?
  2. What must developers configure separately?
  3. Which assumptions from development become invalid in production?
  4. Can developers identify the required changes before deployment?
  5. What must they verify to confirm that the production integration is ready?

These questions help identify gaps between a successful test and a complete deployment.

Why This Matters

When environment differences are unclear, developers may encounter avoidable deployment delays, configuration errors, or unexpected application behaviour.

These outcomes are possibilities, not inevitable consequences of using multiple environments.

These differences are not unusual. Development, testing, and production environments often serve different purposes.

An integration that works in one environment does not automatically work in another.

Consider a developer integrating a payment API.

title: Team-Level LLM API Key Management: The Guide I Wish Someone Gave Me
summary:
When your app was a side project, one .env file with an OpenAI key was fine. The moment a second engineer joins, that setup turns into a small disaster: keys leak into git, a junior's experiment blows the budget, and no one knows who spent what.

Here's the system we ended up with after burning two budgets and rotating three keys.

1. Never share one key across the team

The instinct is to put the production key in 1Password and call it a day. The problem:

  • You can't revoke one person's access without killing everyone's
  • You can't attribute spend
  • When that key leaks (and it will), you rotate it for the whole team

Give each developer their own key. Scope it down.

2. Separate environments from users

Two axes to think about:

Axis Values
Environment dev / staging / prod
Owner each engineer + CI bots

That's a matrix of keys, not one key. A CI key should never have production write access. An intern's dev key should never work in staging.

3. Budget per key, not per account

OpenAI's account-level limit is too coarse — one runaway loop burns everyone's quota. You want per-key spend caps:

# Pseudocode: what the gateway should enforce
per_key_budget = {
  "dev-llong":      {"monthly": 20,  "models": ["gpt-4o-mini"]},
  "prod-service-a": {"monthly": 500, "models": ["gpt-4o","claude-3-5-sonnet"]},
  "ci-bot":         {"monthly": 5,   "models": ["gpt-4o-mini"]},
}

4. Rotate, but make it cheap

Key rotation should be a 5-minute operation, not a sprint. If every rotation means updating 30 service configs, people stop doing it. A gateway layer with one ANTHROPIC_API_KEY-equivalent that routes to upstream providers lets you rotate the upstream key without touching the app.

5. Audit log everything

You want to know, after an incident:

  • Which key made the call
  • Which model and how many tokens
  • From which service

Without this, "who burned $400 last night?" becomes a he-said-she-said.

6. What we actually use

We ran through Envoy + custom Lua scripts, then a vendor-specific dashboard, before landing on a gateway that does per-key budgets, per-model routing, and a unified audit log out of the box. Agent Token is what we use today — one OpenAI-compatible key, per-key spend caps, team usage dashboard across GPT / Claude / Gemini.

The pattern matters more than the tool, though: one key per person per environment, hard budgets, and an audit log you'd actually check.

How does your team manage LLM keys? Genuinely curious what works for bigger orgs.

title: From ISO 27001 to ISO 42001: A Practical AI Governance Implementation Guide
summary:
AI systems introduce governance challenges that traditional information security processes may not fully address. A company can have an established Information Security Management System (ISMS), documented security controls, and an internal audit programme while still lacking processes for AI system impact assessments, model governance, and AI-specific risk management.

This is where ISO/IEC 42001:2023 becomes relevant.

ISO 27001 focuses on information security management, whereas ISO 42001 specifies requirements for establishing and continually improving an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). For engineering teams that already work with ISO 27001, the transition can involve reusing suitable management processes and extending them to cover AI-specific requirements.

The important part is understanding what can be reused, what needs to be added, and how to maintain evidence as AI systems evolve.

Why Does ISO 27001 Alone Not Cover Every AI Governance Requirement?

Information security remains an essential part of AI governance, but it is not the only concern.

Consider an application that uses a third-party language model to process customer requests. The engineering team may already assess access controls, encryption, data confidentiality, and supplier security under its ISMS.

However, additional questions may arise:

  • Can the model produce biased or inappropriate outputs?
  • Are the training or input data suitable for the intended purpose?
  • When should a human review an AI-generated decision?
  • How are changes to the model evaluated before deployment?
  • What documentation is needed to explain the system's behaviour and limitations?
  • How are AI-related risks monitored after release?

These questions require processes that address AI systems and their lifecycle, rather than information security alone.

ISO 42001 provides a management-system framework for organising this work.

What Can Engineering Teams Reuse From ISO 27001?

ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 share the same general harmonized management-system structure across clauses 4 to 10. This creates opportunities to coordinate activities instead of maintaining two completely separate management systems.

1. Risk management workflows

An existing risk register can provide a useful starting point for AI governance.

For example, an engineering team may already document security risks, assign owners, define mitigation measures, and review outstanding issues. These practices can support the AIMS, provided the risk methodology is extended to address relevant AI-related risks and opportunities.

AI-specific assessments may need to consider bias, explainability, data quality, human oversight, and potential impacts on people.

2. Document control and evidence

Many organisations already use version-controlled repositories, ticketing systems, approval workflows, and audit records.

These systems may help maintain AI policies, risk assessments, technical documentation, review decisions, and corrective actions.

The objective is not to create a separate document for every standard. It is to maintain reliable records that can be traced to the requirements they support.

3. Internal audits and management reviews

Existing audit schedules and management review processes may also be coordinated.

However, audit criteria must cover the requirements of both standards. An ISMS audit that focuses only on information security does not automatically establish that an AIMS is effective.

For more detail on shared processes and standard-specific requirements, see the ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 integration guide.

A Practical ISO 42001 Implementation Workflow

A phased approach can help technical teams identify gaps and introduce AI governance without unnecessarily duplicating existing work.

Step 1: Inventory your AI systems

Start by identifying the AI systems used, developed, provided, or deployed within the proposed AIMS scope.

Depending on your organisation, the inventory may include:

  • Internally developed machine learning models
  • Third-party language models and APIs
  • AI-enabled SaaS products
  • Retrieval-augmented generation applications
  • Automated decision-support systems
  • AI components integrated into production services

For each system, record its intended purpose, owner, deployment environment, relevant data sources, external dependencies, and lifecycle status.

This inventory creates a shared reference point for risk assessments, governance decisions, and change management.

Step 2: Define the AIMS scope and responsibilities

Determine which organisational activities and AI systems fall within the management system.

Assign responsibilities across engineering, security, product management, legal, and compliance teams as appropriate.

For example, an ML engineer might maintain model documentation, a security engineer might assess technical vulnerabilities, and a product owner might coordinate reviews of intended use and operational changes.

These are possible organisational arrangements, not job titles mandated by ISO 42001.

Step 3: Perform an AI-specific gap analysis

Compare your current management processes with the requirements of ISO 42001.

Review areas such as:

  • AI policy and governance responsibilities
  • AI risk assessment and treatment
  • AI system impact assessment
  • AI objectives and performance evaluation
  • Data and AI lifecycle management
  • Human oversight and relevant transparency processes
  • Third-party AI relationships
  • Internal audit and continual improvement

Record each gap, the required action, its owner, and the evidence needed to demonstrate implementation.

An existing ISO 27001 certification does not automatically satisfy ISO 42001 requirements.

Teams planning this transition can use the ISO 42001 implementation guide for ISO 27001 holders as a reference for organising implementation phases and identifying areas that require additional work.

Step 4: Assess AI risks and impacts

Risk assessment should reflect the context and intended use of each AI system.

For a customer-facing chatbot, the assessment might examine inaccurate responses, inappropriate disclosures, data handling, and the need for human escalation.

For an AI recruitment system, relevant considerations might include potentially discriminatory outcomes, data representativeness, explainability, and human review.

The assessment process should produce documented findings and decisions. These results can inform risk treatment, AI objectives, and the selection of applicable controls.

ISO 42001 addresses AI system impact assessment as well as AI-related risk management. The two activities should not be treated as interchangeable.

Step 5: Map and implement the controls

Annex A of ISO 42001 contains 38 reference controls organised into nine control objectives.

These objectives cover AI policies, internal organisation, resources, AI system impact assessment, the AI system lifecycle, data, information for interested parties, AI system use, and third-party and customer relationships.

Build a control map that identifies the applicable requirements, current processes, gaps, owners, and supporting evidence.

Where an existing security process supports an AI governance objective, document the relationship. Where it does not cover the relevant requirement, introduce an additional control or process.

The mapping should be based on the actual requirements and the organisation's circumstances, rather than assumptions that similarly named controls are equivalent.

Step 6: Integrate governance into the software development lifecycle

For engineering teams, AI governance is easier to maintain when it connects to existing development workflows.

Consider introducing the following practices:

Before deployment: Review intended use, relevant risks, data considerations, and required approvals.

During development: Maintain model and system documentation, track relevant changes, and record assessment results.

Before significant changes: Evaluate whether a model update, new data source, or change in intended purpose requires another risk or impact assessment.

After deployment: Monitor relevant performance indicators, record incidents, and assign corrective actions where necessary.

The exact controls depend on the system, its context, and applicable requirements. ISO 42001 does not prescribe a single CI/CD implementation for every AI application.

Step 7: Audit and improve the management system

Conduct an internal audit against the applicable ISO 42001 requirements and defined audit criteria.

Review the implementation of controls, the quality of evidence, assigned responsibilities, and the operation of risk and impact assessment processes.

Management review should evaluate the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the AIMS. Track findings and corrective actions rather than treating the audit as the final step.

Organisations seeking certification should coordinate with an appropriate certification body.

How Can Teams Manage AI Governance Evidence?

A common operational problem is that evidence becomes scattered across Git repositories, spreadsheets, project management tools, shared drives, and approval systems.

This can make it difficult to determine which AI systems have been assessed, who approved a decision, and whether the supporting documentation is current.

A central evidence structure can help.

For example, an organisation might maintain the following relationships:

  • AI system inventory → identifies the system and its owner.
  • Risk assessment → records identified risks and treatment decisions.
  • Control mapping → connects requirements to implemented processes.
  • Technical documentation → describes relevant system characteristics and limitations.
  • Approval records → establish who reviewed and authorised a decision.
  • Monitoring records → provide evidence of ongoing review and improvement.

These relationships can be maintained in existing tools or supported by dedicated AI governance software.

The objective is traceability: teams should be able to move from an AI system to its relevant assessments, controls, decisions, and evidence without reconstructing the history manually.

Where Does the EU AI Act Fit Into ISO 42001?

ISO 42001 is a voluntary management-system standard, while the EU AI Act establishes legal obligations for relevant AI systems and actors.

An AIMS can support governance processes, documentation, and risk management. However, ISO 42001 certification alone does not establish compliance with the EU AI Act.

Organisations must separately determine their applicable legal obligations, including relevant requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency, AI literacy, and other provisions where applicable.

The legal roles of provider and deployer also need to be assessed under the EU AI Act. They should not be inferred solely from an organisation's internal governance responsibilities.

For teams coordinating management-system work with regulatory requirements, an integrated approach can reduce duplicated effort while preserving the distinction between voluntary standards and legal obligations.

Can AI Compliance Software Support the Implementation?

AI governance software can help organisations connect AI inventories, risk assessments, control mappings, and evidence records in one workflow.

AnnexOps is one option for teams managing ISO 42001, ISO 27001, and EU AI Act compliance operations. Its ISO 27001 compliance solution describes support for ISMS scope, risk registers, controls, evidence, and internal audits.

Software selection should depend on the organisation's scope, existing tools, evidence requirements, and workflow needs. A platform can support compliance operations, but it does not replace management accountability, legal assessment, or an independent certification audit.

Final Thoughts

Moving from ISO 27001 to ISO 42001 is an extension of management-system capabilities, not simply a change in security documentation.

Engineering and compliance teams can make the transition more manageable by inventorying AI systems, defining responsibilities, assessing AI-specific risks and impacts, mapping controls, and maintaining traceable evidence.

The most sustainable approach is to connect governance activities to the software lifecycle and existing management processes while preserving the requirements unique to each standard.

For a detailed phase-by-phase roadmap, read the ISO 42001 implementation guide for organisations that already have ISO 27001.

title: Contract Testing for Microservices: Catch API Integration Issues Early
summary:
Microservices allow teams to develop and deploy components independently. That independence becomes harder to maintain when one service changes an API and another service still expects the old behavior.

A provider might rename a response field, change a data type, or introduce a new validation rule. Its own unit tests may pass, yet a consumer can still fail when it receives an unexpected response.

Contract testing helps catch these compatibility problems before they reach production. It verifies that services continue to meet the expectations they have agreed to support.

What does contract testing verify?

An API contract describes how one service interacts with another. Depending on the interface, it may define request fields, response structures, data types, status codes, and expected behavior.

Consider an order service that calls a payment service. The order service sends a payment request and expects a response containing a transaction identifier and a payment status.

If the payment service changes the response field from transactionId to paymentReference, the payment service may still pass its own tests. But the order service could fail if it continues looking for the original field.

A contract test can detect this mismatch by checking whether the provider's behavior still satisfies the consumer's expectations.

Contract testing is not a complete replacement for integration testing. It verifies compatibility at defined interaction boundaries, while integration and end-to-end tests can reveal problems involving broader workflows, infrastructure, timing, and real dependencies.

Consumer-driven contract testing

One common approach is consumer-driven contract testing.

In this model, a consumer defines the interactions it relies on. Those expectations are captured in a contract that the provider can verify.

A typical workflow looks like this:

  1. The consumer test describes a request and the response it expects.
  2. A contract is generated and shared through an agreed repository or contract broker.
  3. The provider verifies that it can satisfy the published contract.
  4. Compatibility checks run as part of the development and release pipeline.
  5. Teams review contract verification results before deploying potentially incompatible changes.

title: What Is the Highest-Paying Blockchain Certification?
summary:
Blockchain professionals are increasingly exploring specialized certifications to strengthen their skills, qualify for advanced roles, and pursue better-paying opportunities. However, there is no single blockchain certification that guarantees the highest salary. Earning potential depends on your technical expertise, work experience, location, and the role you target.

The most valuable certification is often the one that aligns with a high-demand specialization, such as blockchain architecture, smart contract development, or blockchain security.

Which Blockchain Certifications Can Support Higher-Paying Careers?

Several certifications are worth considering based on your career goals:

Blockchain Architect: The Certified Enterprise Blockchain Architect (CEBA) from 101 Blockchains focuses on enterprise blockchain architecture and solution design. It may suit professionals targeting blockchain architect or enterprise consultant roles.

Blockchain Professional: The Certified Enterprise Blockchain Professional (CEBP) from 101 Blockchains covers enterprise blockchain concepts and applications, making it an option for professionals seeking a broader understanding of business use cases.

Blockchain Developer: Developer-focused certifications can help learners build knowledge of blockchain applications, smart contracts, and decentralized technologies. These are relevant to Web3 development careers.

Blockchain Security Specialist: Security-focused training can help professionals develop skills in identifying vulnerabilities and understanding smart contract risks, which are important in blockchain security roles.

Which Certification Is Best for Your Career?

The right choice depends on your professional goals. For enterprise consulting and architecture, CEBA is worth exploring. For broader business knowledge, CEBP may be a better starting point. Developers should prioritize hands-on smart contract experience, while security professionals should focus on blockchain vulnerabilities and auditing.

You can explore these programs through the 101 Blockchains certification catalog.

Do Blockchain Certifications Increase Salaries?

A certification can strengthen your résumé and demonstrate specialized knowledge, but it does not automatically lead to a salary increase. Employers also evaluate practical experience, coding ability, problem-solving skills, and the ability to deliver real projects. Salary estimates vary considerably by role, country, and experience level, so advertised figures should be treated as indicative rather than guaranteed.

Final Thoughts

There is no universally highest-paying blockchain certification. The strongest option is the credential that helps you qualify for your target role and demonstrate job-ready skills. Consider enterprise blockchain architecture, development, or security based on your interests, and complement your certification with practical projects.

title: How Forward-Deployed Engineering Is Rewriting Enterprise AI Delivery
summary:
Forward-Deployed Engineering: An Overview

Enterprise AI has reached a familiar and costly plateau. Models are more capable than ever. Cloud platforms and open-source tooling have removed many barriers to experimentation. Yet the majority of organizations still struggle to move from promising pilots to production systems that deliver measurable business outcomes. According to Atlassian’s research, 85 percent of knowledge workers now use AI, but only 6 percent of executives can point to clear, organization-wide ROI. McKinsey’s surveys similarly show high adoption rates alongside a stubbornly small share of companies reporting material EBIT impact. The bottleneck is no longer model quality. It is the last mile: integrating AI into messy real-world data, workflows, governance constraints, and operational systems. Forward-deployed engineering (FDE) has emerged as the operating model that addresses this gap. Originally pioneered by Palantir and now adopted at scale by AWS, Atlassian, Databricks, Deloitte, OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, FDE embeds senior engineers directly inside customer environments. These engineers do not write recommendations or build throwaway prototypes. They write production code, own outcomes, and leave the customer stronger than they found it. This approach is reshaping how enterprises adopt and scale AI.

Why Traditional Delivery Models Fall Short for FDE

Forward-deployed engineering addresses the structural gaps in traditional software delivery and consulting models, which assume relatively stable requirements and deterministic systems. An organization defines needs, a vendor or integrator builds against a scope of work, and ownership transfers at go-live. AI systems break these assumptions. They are probabilistic. Their performance depends heavily on the quality and relevance of organizational context, the structure of upstream processes, and continuous evaluation against real outcomes. Many of the highest-value opportunities only become visible once engineers work inside the live environment. Common failure patterns include:

  • Pilots that succeed in controlled sandboxes but collapse under production data volumes, latency requirements, or security constraints.
  • Handoffs between strategy consultants, data scientists, and engineering teams that lose critical context.
  • Solutions that optimize for model accuracy rather than end-to-end workflow impact.
  • Internal teams that lack specialized experience to productionize agentic systems safely and at scale, often neglecting the essential agent harness orchestration layer that enables multi-step tool execution.

The result is a growing inventory of underused models and limited returns on substantial AI investment.

Industry Context: From Niche Practice to Mainstream Investment

Palantir formalized the forward-deployed engineer role in the mid-to-late 2000s. Facing customers in intelligence and defense who could not fully articulate requirements or share data freely, the company sent engineers to work on site. Internally, these engineers were known as “Deltas.” Their mandate was clear: one customer, many capabilities. Product engineers focused on one capability across many customers. The field-to-product feedback loop became a core advantage. Until around 2016, Palantir employed more forward-deployed engineers than traditional product engineers. The model later spread as alumni and industry observers recognized its value for complex enterprise software. In 2025 and 2026, the model accelerated rapidly as AI deployment became the primary constraint. AWS announced a dedicated Forward Deployed Engineering organization backed by a $1 billion investment, with the explicit goal of embedding engineers to co-develop agentic AI solutions and leave customers self-sufficient. Atlassian launched its own FDE program, reporting work with more than 100 enterprise customers and more than 80 production AI agents. Databricks formalized an FDE organization focused on accelerating business outcomes with its platform. Deloitte, Tredence, and others have followed with similar offerings. The common thread is recognition that the hardest problems in enterprise AI live at the intersection of technology, process, and organizational reality.

What Forward-Deployed Engineering Actually Is

A forward-deployed engineer is a customer-facing software engineer employed by a platform or AI vendor (or, in some cases, a specialized services firm). The engineer embeds with a customer team for a defined period, works inside the customer’s systems and data environment, and is measured on production outcomes rather than deliverables or billable hours. Key distinctions from adjacent roles:

The defining characteristic is the closed loop. FDEs solve the customer’s immediate problem while capturing reusable patterns, integration approaches, and domain insights that improve the underlying platform for future customers. In many software engineering teams, this integration relies heavily on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as standard plumbing for connecting agents to external tools and data stores.

How the Forward-Deployed Engineering Model Works in Practice

Successful FDE engagements typically follow a structured yet flexible sequence:

  1. Outcome definition – Start with a high-impact business problem and clear success criteria rather than a technology request, often anchored by a robust Forward Deployed Engineering framework.
  2. Embedded discovery – Engineers join the customer’s standups, access real systems (under appropriate controls), and map the actual workflow, data flows, permissions, and failure points.
  3. Build and iterate in production context – Develop agents, integrations, evaluation harnesses, and supporting infrastructure that fit the customer’s environment. Work happens in short cycles with continuous feedback, utilizing spec-driven development to ensure generated code strictly adheres to requirements.
  4. Adoption and transfer – Create playbooks, governance patterns, and training so the customer team can establish a Center of Excellence (CoE) and operate the solution independently.
  5. Feedback to product – Capture what’s generalized and feed field insights back into the core platform or shared libraries.

AWS emphasizes compressing timelines from months to days or weeks while ensuring self-sufficiency. Atlassian’s approach targets roughly 12 weeks to measurable value and self-sufficient teams. Databricks pairs FDE work with its Lakehouse platform and partner network.

How CapeStart Delivers Forward-Deployed AI Engineering

CapeStart’s Forward-Deployed AI Engineering services embed experienced engineers within the customer’s environment to design, build, integrate, and operationalize AI solutions alongside internal teams. The engagement covers deep discovery, rapid prototyping, production implementation, training, joint operations, and continuous engineering support. Rather than stopping after deployment, CapeStart’s engineers can remain embedded to monitor performance, adapt workflows, expand capabilities, and support the system as business requirements evolve. The model supports AI agents, RAG systems, enterprise integrations, data engineering, automation, cloud platforms, and governance across regulated and operationally complex environments. Learn more about CapeStart’s Forward-Deployed AI Engineering services.

Key Benefits and Outcomes of Forward Deployed Engineering

When executed well, the model delivers several advantages:

  • Faster time to production value – Engineers work inside constraints rather than discovering them after the fact.
  • Higher relevance – Solutions address the real process, not a sanitized version of it.
  • Knowledge transfer – Customers retain capability rather than remaining dependent.
  • Product improvement – Vendors gain ground-truth signal that pure product teams rarely obtain.
  • Measurable impact – Success is defined by business metrics such as reduced resolution time, hours saved, or process cycle time.

Published examples include Atlassian customers achieving multi-million-dollar savings through autonomous triage agents, significant reductions in triage effort, and thousands of hours saved annually through production agents. Databricks has reported outcomes such as doubled search success rates and large-scale data migrations completed in months rather than longer traditional timelines. These results are not universal. They depend on selecting high-value use cases, securing executive sponsorship, and maintaining strong collaboration between FDE and customer teams.

Use Cases

The model is particularly effective for:

  • Complex agentic workflows that span multiple systems (IT service management, customer support, content operations, supply chain decisioning).
  • Regulated industries such as pharma, medical imaging, and healthcare enterprises requiring strict compliance (e.g., FDA 21 CFR Part 11, HIPAA, GDPR) and secure system integrations.
  • Organizations that have strong domain expertise but limited internal capacity for production AI engineering.
  • Platform vendors seeking to accelerate adoption of sophisticated capabilities that require deep integration.

It is less necessary for straightforward API consumption or simple chat interfaces that require minimal customization.

Best Practices

  1. Define success in business terms before the engagement begins.
  2. Ensure strong internal ownership and pairing with the FDE team. The goal is capability transfer, not permanent dependency.
  3. Prioritize use cases where process redesign and system integration matter more than pure model performance. For specialized tasks, leverage specialized models like Jev for ultra-fast, low-cost classification alongside LLMs.
  4. Establish clear data access, security, and evaluation frameworks early.
  5. Plan the knowledge-transfer phase from day one rather than treating it as an afterthought.
  6. Measure both the immediate outcome and the residual capability left behind.

Limitations

FDE is not a universal solution. It is expensive relative to pure software licenses because it allocates senior engineering talent to individual customers. Scalability is constrained by the supply of engineers who combine strong technical skills with customer-facing judgment and domain adaptability. There is also a risk of the model being diluted. When the title is applied to roles that primarily perform demos, configuration, or advisory work without production ownership or product feedback, the distinctive value disappears. Some observers note that without the closed loop back into product development, the role becomes closer to traditional professional services. Organizations must also manage the cultural and operational impact of external engineers working inside sensitive environments. Clear agreements on IP, data handling, and exit criteria are essential.

Future Trends in Forward Deployed Engineering

Several developments are likely to shape the next phase:

  • Greater use of multi-agent architectures and agentic systems by FDE teams themselves to accelerate delivery and control costs.
  • Stronger emphasis on semantic layers, ontologies, and enterprise context graphs that make AI agents more reliable.
  • Hybrid models that combine vendor FDEs with scaled partner networks.
  • Internal adoption of forward-deployed practices inside large enterprises, sometimes called “business engineering” or similar terms.
  • Continued pressure on pure consulting models that lack deep production engineering capability.

As platforms mature and more reusable patterns emerge, the intensity of per-customer engineering may decrease for certain classes of problems. For the highest-value and most complex AI systems, however, proximity to the real environment will remain decisive.

Conclusion

Forward-deployed engineering addresses the central challenge of enterprise AI in 2026: turning capable models into reliable, governed, outcome-driving systems inside real organizations. By embedding engineers who own production results and feed learning back into platforms, the model closes the gap that has left many AI initiatives stuck in pilot mode. It is not magic and it is not free. It requires the right talent, clear outcomes, and disciplined knowledge transfer. When those conditions are met, it provides a practical path from AI activity to measurable business impact. Organizations evaluating their AI operating model should examine whether their current delivery approach still matches the nature of the systems they are trying to build. In many cases, the last mile is where the real work and the real value now reside. For teams exploring this approach, start by identifying one high-friction workflow with clear business ownership and measurable success criteria. That focused starting point often reveals more about readiness than any high-level strategy document.

title: How Does AWS Control Who Can Access What? Understanding IAM Policies, Roles & Least Privilege

When I started learning AWS, I realized something important: creating cloud resources is only part of the job. We also need to control who can access those resources, what they can do, and which AWS services can communicate with each other.

Imagine deploying a MERN application on AWS. Your backend needs to read files from S3, retrieve database credentials, and write application logs. Should we give it full access to our AWS account?

Definitely not.

This is where AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) becomes essential.

In this article, I'll explore IAM users, groups, roles, policies, trust policies, permission boundaries, and the principle of least privilege using practical examples.

Figure: Understanding AWS IAM through identities, permissions, and a real-world application example.

1. What Is AWS IAM?

AWS IAM is a service that helps control access to AWS resources.

It answers three fundamental questions:

  • Who is making the request?
  • What actions are they allowed to perform?
  • Which resources can they access?

For example, a developer might be allowed to view EC2 instances but not delete production databases. Meanwhile, an application running on Amazon ECS might need permission to read a specific file from S3.

IAM lets us define these permissions instead of granting everyone unrestricted access.

2. Understanding the Main IAM Components

IAM users

An IAM user represents an identity with long-term credentials, when those credentials are configured.

For example, a developer may have an IAM user that can access specific development resources.

However, for people, AWS recommends federation and temporary credentials where practical rather than creating long-term IAM user credentials for everyday access.

Important: Avoid using the AWS root user for routine tasks. Protect it carefully and use it only when root-level access is specifically required.

IAM groups

An IAM group allows you to manage permissions for multiple IAM users together.

For example:

  • Developers — access to development resources
  • Auditors — read-only access for reviewing resources
  • Administrators — broader administrative permissions

Groups simplify permission management, but they are not a replacement for carefully designed policies.

IAM roles

An IAM role is an identity that provides a set of permissions and can be assumed by an authorized principal.

Roles are especially useful when AWS services need to communicate securely.

Imagine an application running on Amazon EC2 that needs to read a file from S3.

Instead of placing AWS access keys inside the application code, we can attach an appropriate IAM role to the EC2 instance. The application can then obtain temporary credentials through the AWS-provided credential mechanism.

This reduces the need to store long-term credentials in the application.

IAM roles are also used with ECS tasks, Lambda functions, and many other AWS services.

IAM policies

An IAM policy is a document that defines permissions.

A policy can specify:

  • Effect: Allow or Deny
  • Action: The operation being requested
  • Resource: The AWS resource involved
  • Condition: Optional requirements that must be satisfied

For example, an application might need permission to download objects from one S3 bucket without being allowed to delete them.

A simplified policy could look like this:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-documents/*"
    }
  ]
}

This allows the specified GetObject operation on objects in the named bucket. It does not, by itself, grant permission to upload or delete objects.

Replace the example bucket name with your actual resource when implementing a policy.

3. Identity-Based vs. Resource-Based Policies

AWS supports different ways of defining access.

Identity-based policies attach to identities such as users, groups, and roles. They describe what those identities can do.

Resource-based policies attach to supported resources and describe which principals can access them.

For example, an IAM role may have permission to read objects from an S3 bucket, while the bucket policy may also restrict which principals are allowed to access that bucket.

Both sides can matter. An Allow in one policy does not automatically override an applicable explicit Deny or other access restrictions.

4. What Is a Trust Policy?

This is one of the most important distinctions when learning IAM roles.

An IAM role has two separate questions to answer:

  1. Trust policy: Who is allowed to assume this role?
  2. Permissions policy: What can the role do after it is assumed?

Imagine an ECS task that needs to access an S3 bucket.

The task role's trust policy establishes that the appropriate ECS tasks can assume the role. Its permissions policy grants only the required S3 actions.

These policies solve different problems. Allowing a service to assume a role does not automatically give that role permission to access S3.

5. How IAM Works in a Real Application

Let's use a simplified architecture for a web application deployed on AWS.

                Developer
                    |
                    v
              AWS Console / CLI
                    |
                    v
               IAM Identity
                    |
            IAM Policies
                    |
                    v
             AWS Resources


          Application Running on ECS
                    |
                    v
               ECS Task Role
                    |
            Permissions Policy
                    |
          +---------+----------+
          |                    |
          v                    v
      Amazon S3        AWS Secrets Manager

The developer accesses AWS using an authorized identity. The application accesses other AWS services through its task role.

These are separate identities with separate permissions.

For example:

  • A developer can deploy a new application version.
  • An ECS task can read specific S3 objects.
  • The task can retrieve a particular secret if its role is authorized to do so.
  • Neither identity automatically needs full administrator access.

This is the basic idea behind secure access control in cloud applications.

6. What Is the Principle of Least Privilege?

The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task.

Suppose your application needs to read files from S3.

A poor approach would be to grant s3:* on every bucket in the account.

A better approach would be to grant only the necessary S3 actions on the specific bucket or objects the application needs.

Broad permission Least-privilege alternative
All S3 actions Only required S3 actions
All resources Specific resource ARNs where supported
Permanent credentials Temporary credentials where practical
Administrator access for every developer Role-based access suited to each responsibility

Least privilege is not simply about writing smaller policies. It also means reviewing permissions regularly, removing unused access, and considering what could happen if an identity were compromised.

7. What Are Permission Boundaries?

Permission boundaries help set the maximum permissions that an IAM user or role can receive through identity-based policies.

Think of them as a permissions ceiling.

For example, an organization might allow a development team to create roles for its applications but require that those roles remain within a defined permissions boundary.

A boundary does not grant permissions by itself. The identity still needs applicable policies that allow the requested actions.

Also, a permissions boundary is not a universal restriction on every possible access path. Resource-based policies and other AWS authorization rules must be considered when evaluating effective access.

8. IAM Roles vs. Hardcoded Credentials

Consider two approaches for an application that accesses AWS services.

Approach A: Hardcoded credentials 

const accessKey = "YOUR_ACCESS_KEY";
const secretKey = "YOUR_SECRET_KEY";

This is unsafe. Credentials can accidentally enter Git repositories, logs, build artifacts, or shared files.

Approach B: IAM role and temporary credentials

Configure the application's execution environment with the appropriate IAM role. Use the AWS SDK's default credential provider chain to obtain credentials.

For example, with AWS SDK for JavaScript v3:

import { S3Client, ListObjectsV2Command } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";

const s3 = new S3Client({
  region: "ap-south-1"
});

const response = await s3.send(
  new ListObjectsV2Command({
    Bucket: "my-app-documents"
  })
);

console.log(response.Contents);

The SDK can obtain credentials from the supported runtime credential provider chain, including the role credentials provided in an appropriately configured AWS environment.

The example still requires permission for s3:ListBucket on the bucket. If the application only needs to download a known object, grant s3:GetObject on that object instead.

Remember: Using an IAM role does not automatically make an application secure. The role must have the right trust relationship and narrowly scoped permissions.

9. IAM and AWS Secrets Manager

IAM and Secrets Manager work together, but they have different responsibilities.

  • IAM controls whether an identity can perform an action.
  • AWS Secrets Manager stores and manages sensitive values such as database credentials and API keys.

For example, an ECS task can use its task role to retrieve a particular database secret from Secrets Manager. The task role should not be allowed to retrieve every secret in the account unless that broader access is genuinely required.

Avoid embedding secrets in source code, Docker images, or GitHub repositories.

10. Common IAM Mistakes to Avoid

Here are a few mistakes worth watching for when building AWS projects:

  1. Using the root user for everyday development.
  2. Giving applications administrator permissions.
  3. Hardcoding AWS access keys into source code.
  4. Confusing a role's trust policy with its permissions policy.
  5. Assuming a permissions boundary grants access.
  6. Forgetting that an explicit Deny can override an Allow.
  7. Granting access to every resource when only one resource is required.
  8. Leaving unused users, access keys, or permissions in place.

IAM policies should be tested and reviewed carefully, particularly before making changes in production.

11. What Should You Remember for the AWS SAA-C03 Exam?

These are useful distinctions to remember:

  • IAM user: An identity that can have long-term credentials.
  • IAM group: Organizes IAM users for permission management.
  • IAM role: An assumable identity commonly used for temporary credentials.
  • IAM policy: Defines permissions.
  • Trust policy: Defines who can assume a role.
  • Permissions boundary: Sets a maximum permission boundary for an IAM identity.
  • Least privilege: Grants only the access needed.
  • Explicit Deny: Overrides an applicable Allow.
  • Instance profile: A mechanism used to pass an IAM role to an EC2 instance.
  • ECS task role: Grants permissions to application code running in an ECS task.
  • ECS task execution role: Grants permissions needed by the ECS agent to perform tasks such as pulling images and sending logs, depending on configuration.

That last distinction matters: the task role is for the application; the execution role is for ECS task startup and management operations.

Final Thoughts

Learning IAM changed how I think about deploying applications on AWS. It is not enough for an application to work — it must also have the right permissions and nothing more than it needs.

Whether you're deploying a Lambda function, running containers on ECS, or building a larger cloud architecture, IAM is one of the foundations of secure AWS development.

My biggest takeaway is simple: don't ask only whether an application can access a resource. Ask whether it should have that access, and whether the permission can be made more specific.

That's the mindset behind least privilege.

I'm continuing my AWS learning journey and documenting the concepts that help me understand how real cloud systems are built and secured.

title: DPDP Engineering Checklist: 10 Steps to Protect Personal Data
summary:
Introduction

India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, and the DPDP Rules, 2025, make personal data protection an important consideration for businesses building and operating digital applications. For engineering teams, preparing for DPDP requirements involves more than updating privacy policies. It requires examining how personal data is collected, processed, stored, accessed and shared across an application's architecture.

Consider a typical product workflow. A customer enters their phone number into an application. The backend processes the request, an analytics service records the event, and an error-monitoring tool captures request details during debugging. The primary database may be secure, but the same personal information could now exist in several other systems.

This creates an important engineering challenge: protecting personal data throughout its lifecycle, not just where it is originally stored.

Developers, DevOps engineers, security teams and engineering managers need to understand where personal data flows, which services can access it, how long it is retained and what happens when a user exercises an applicable data protection right.

A practical DPDP engineering checklist helps teams identify gaps, assign responsibilities and build appropriate safeguards into everyday development workflows.

This article covers ten areas to review when preparing applications for DPDP requirements, including data mapping, purpose limitation, consent management, PII protection, access control, application logs, deletion workflows, third-party integrations, breach response and privacy testing.

For a broader overview of how data protection controls fit into application architecture, see Securelytix's guide to DPDP and AI workflows.

The DPDP Engineering Checklist

1. Map Personal Data Across Your Application

You cannot protect personal data effectively without knowing where it goes.

Start by identifying the personal data your application collects, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, identity details and other information that can identify an individual. Then trace how that information moves between application components and external services.

Engineering checklist:

  • Identify personal data collected by every application and API.
  • Map data flows between frontend services, backend systems and databases.
  • Identify copies in caches, message queues, analytics platforms and backups.
  • Document which internal services and third-party vendors can access personal data.
  • Review AI workflows, including prompts, tool calls and retrieval systems.

Maintain an up-to-date data inventory and data flow diagram. These help engineering teams understand where personal information is processed and where additional security controls may be necessary.

2. Apply Purpose Limitation and Data Minimisation

Collecting more information than a product needs increases the amount of data that must be protected. The DPDP framework addresses processing for lawful purposes and limits personal data processing to what is necessary for the specified purpose.

Engineering checklist:

  • Collect only the personal data required for the intended purpose.
  • Avoid returning unnecessary personal fields from APIs.
  • Remove redundant personal information from event payloads.
  • Review whether analytics systems need identifiable customer data.
  • Define retention periods and implement appropriate deletion processes.

For example, an order-status API may only need an order ID and delivery status. Returning the customer's complete address, phone number and payment details increases exposure without necessarily improving the functionality.

Data minimisation should be considered during API design, database modelling and product development, rather than added after deployment.

3. Build Consent and Privacy Controls Into the Application

Consent management should not be limited to a checkbox or banner on the frontend. Where consent is the applicable basis for processing, the backend and connected services must handle consent status and withdrawal appropriately.

Engineering checklist:

  • Present clear privacy notices explaining the purpose of data collection.
  • Record consent and relevant changes in an auditable manner.
  • Connect consent status to systems that process personal data.
  • Implement workflows for withdrawing consent.
  • Support applicable requests for access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal.

Test these controls across APIs, background jobs and third-party integrations, not just the user interface. A withdrawal option is ineffective if downstream services continue processing data without an applicable legal basis.

4. Protect PII With Appropriate Security Controls

The DPDP Rules, 2025, Rule 6 addresses reasonable security safeguards for protecting personal data. Engineering teams should evaluate security controls according to the sensitivity of the information, the application's architecture and the risks involved.

Engineering checklist:

  • Encrypt personal data in transit and at rest.
  • Apply masking or redaction when original values are unnecessary.
  • Evaluate tokenization for sensitive fields used across services.
  • Restrict access to encryption keys and systems holding original data.
  • Test safeguards against unauthorised access and data exposure.

For example, an internal service may need to identify a customer without receiving their actual phone number. Tokenization can replace the original value with a token while keeping the mapping in a separately protected system.

PII tokenization is one approach to reducing unnecessary exposure of original personal information across application workflows. The original values remain protected in a controlled vault while supported systems can work with tokenized representations.

Tokenization is one possible security measure, not a complete DPDP compliance solution. Its effectiveness depends on implementation, access controls and protection of the original data.

5. Enforce Access Control Across Services

Personal data should only be accessible to authorised users and services for legitimate purposes. Even a well-protected database can expose information if an API returns unnecessary fields or a service account has excessive privileges.

Engineering checklist:

  • Apply role-based access control (RBAC) or attribute-based access policies where appropriate.
  • Follow the principle of least privilege for employees and service accounts.
  • Restrict access to production databases and sensitive endpoints.
  • Secure service-to-service communication.
  • Review permissions regularly and revoke unnecessary access.

Access controls should cover internal APIs, cloud infrastructure, data pipelines and third-party integrations. Review them whenever application responsibilities or system permissions change.

For an example of how tokenization, controlled data access and auditability can work together, see Securelytix's security architecture.

6. Prevent Personal Data Leaks Through Logs and AI Workflows

Application logs, traces and monitoring tools can unintentionally collect personal information during routine debugging. AI workflows introduce additional risks when applications send customer details to model providers, external tools or retrieval systems.

Engineering checklist:

  • Avoid logging raw request bodies containing personal data.
  • Redact sensitive fields before sending events to monitoring platforms.
  • Review information captured in traces and error reports.
  • Minimise personal data included in AI prompts and tool calls.
  • Restrict access to vector databases, cached responses and conversation histories.
  • Review third-party data retention and deletion practices.

Engineering principle: Protect personal data before it reaches a downstream system.

For AI-enabled applications, this means considering the entire request path, from the application backend to model providers, agent tools, logs and retrieval systems. A data privacy vault is one architectural approach for keeping original sensitive values separate from the representations used by downstream services.

Shared middleware, API gateways and reusable data-handling libraries can help enforce these controls consistently across applications.

7. Establish Data Retention and Deletion Workflows

Deleting a record from the primary database does not guarantee that every copy has been removed. Personal data may remain in caches, search indexes, exports, backups or third-party systems.

Engineering checklist:

  • Define retention periods based on processing purposes and applicable legal obligations.
  • Automate deletion when required conditions are met.
  • Propagate relevant deletion requests to downstream systems.
  • Define how expired data is handled in backups and archives.
  • Maintain appropriate evidence of completed deletion workflows.

The DPDP framework addresses erasure subject to applicable legal requirements and exceptions. Engineering teams should therefore design deletion as a coordinated workflow, rather than relying on a single database operation.

8. Secure Third-Party Processors and Integrations

Modern applications rely on cloud platforms, payment gateways, analytics tools and external APIs. Sharing personal data with these services creates additional risks that engineering teams must account for.

Under Section 8 of the DPDP Act, a Data Fiduciary remains responsible for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf. Engagement of a Data Processor must also be supported by a valid contract.

Engineering checklist:

  • Maintain an inventory of vendors processing personal data.
  • Review vendor security controls and data-handling practices.
  • Ensure relevant contracts address applicable security requirements.
  • Restrict the personal data shared with each integration.
  • Establish processes for vendor incidents and data deletion.

Avoid sending complete customer records to third-party services when only a few fields are necessary. Review integrations whenever vendors, data flows or processing purposes change.

9. Prepare for Personal Data Breaches

Even well-designed security controls cannot eliminate every risk. Engineering teams need an incident response process to identify potential breaches, investigate their impact and coordinate the required notifications.

Engineering checklist:

  • Configure alerts for suspicious access and potential data exposure.
  • Define incident ownership and escalation procedures.
  • Preserve evidence and investigate affected systems and data.
  • Establish procedures for required notifications to affected individuals and the Data Protection Board of India.
  • Conduct incident response simulations to identify gaps.

The DPDP Rules, 2025, prescribe personal data breach notification requirements. Engineering teams should map their response procedures to the applicable timelines and requirements rather than relying on informal internal reporting.

10. Integrate Privacy Testing Into the Development Lifecycle

Privacy safeguards can break when developers introduce new APIs, features, integrations or infrastructure changes. A one-time security review cannot account for every future change.

Engineering checklist:

  • Include personal data exposure scenarios in code reviews.
  • Test access controls, masking and deletion behaviour.
  • Avoid using real personal data in development and testing environments unless appropriately justified and protected.
  • Review data flows before deploying new integrations.
  • Reassess safeguards after significant architectural changes.

Where practical, incorporate privacy-related tests into CI/CD pipelines. Automated checks can help detect accidental exposure, unauthorised access and regressions before new code reaches production.

Turn the DPDP Engineering Checklist Into Action

A checklist becomes useful when each item has an owner, a defined implementation plan and a way to verify completion.

Begin by mapping personal data flows, then prioritise risks such as excessive collection, uncontrolled access, exposed logs and unnecessary third-party sharing. Assign responsibilities across application engineering, DevOps, security and product teams.

Track each control as Not Started, In Progress or Verified, and maintain evidence such as:

  • Data flow diagrams
  • Access reviews
  • Test results
  • Deletion records

Revisit the checklist as the application evolves. Privacy protection should be part of the development lifecycle, not a final approval step before release.

Conclusion

Preparing for DPDP compliance requires more than updating privacy policies. Engineering teams need visibility into personal data flows, appropriate security safeguards, controlled access, reliable deletion workflows and tested incident response procedures.
